plain_claim: In a join-semilattice with bottom satisfying the ascending chain condition (ACC), if every transfer function distributes over binary joins and every node unreachable from the entry has a strict transfer function (f u ⊥ = ⊥), then the dataflow inequations have a least solution, and for every least solution x and every node v, x v is a least upper bound of the values of all paths from the entry to v (MFP = MOP). plain_claim: In a join-semilattice with bottom L (L.IsJSL), consider the five-node diamond CFG: an entry node with initial value a ∈ I and transfer id, two single-node branches with transfers g, h ∈ F, a join node with transfer f ∈ F, and an exit node. (i) If every f ∈ F distributes over every realizable pair (g a, h a) with g, h ∈ F and a ∈ I, then on every such diamond every least solution equals MOP at every node (without a monotonicity hypothesis). (ii) Conversely, if every member of F is monotone and every such diamond is exact, then F distributes over every realizable pair. (iii) If F contains every constant function, I is non-empty, and either every member of F is monotone or L satisfies the ascending chain condition, then exactness on all such diamonds is equivalent to full distributivity of every member of F (in the ascending-chain case, exactness on all such diamonds forces every member of F to be monotone: monotone_of_diamondExact_of_acc_of_const_mem_of_nonempty). The entry transfer is fixed to id whatever F is.

tier_justification: Kildall's Theorem 1 (termination) and the least-fixed-point property of the worklist result are classical, and least-ness of a Kildall-style iteration is mechanized in Isabelle (JinjaThreads, kildall_properties) and Coq (rocq-archive/kildall, monotone_step_imp_kildall_dfa). plain_claim: For a join-semilattice with bottom L (L.IsJSL) with a decidable order test, the fuel-bounded worklist solver kildall L G fuel (start with init at the entry and ⊥ elsewhere, all nodes on the worklist; popping u joins f u (x u) into each successor whose value it does not already lie below and pushes that successor; one unit of fuel per pop) satisfies: whenever it returns some x, x is a solution of the inequations (for any transfer functions) and, if the transfers are monotone, the least solution; on a lattice of height at most h it returns some value whenever fuel ≥ n * (h + 1) + 1, with or without monotonicity; together, with monotone transfers and that fuel, it returns some x and x is the least solution (MFP). The fuel bound is attained for every n ≥ 1 and h ≥ 0 (kildall_fuel_bound_attained: on a CFG of n nodes, each with a self-loop, with monotone transfers over a chain of height h, fuel n * (h + 1) returns none).

One unit of `fuel` in `kildall` pays for popping one node `u` and running `propagate` across all entries of `succs G u`; thus `fuel ≥ n * (h + 1) + 1` bounds outer worklist pops rather than individual edge propagations (`O(|G.edges|)` join and order checks per pop, including duplicate edges).

The ascending chain condition alone gives no uniform fuel bound (kildall_acc_has_no_uniform_fuel), although it suffices for the existence of the least solution (exists_isLeastSolution_of_monotone_of_acc).

All-nodes worklist seeding vs entry-only seeding trades global inequation satisfaction against unreachable-code isolation: seeding all nodes (`kildall`) guarantees a global `IsSolution` without strictness (even without monotonicity, `kildall_isSolution_of_eq_some`) but allows non-strict unreachable nodes to over-approximate reachable nodes (`exactness_needs_unreachableStrict`), whereas seeding only the entry avoids unreachable-node propagation and solves the reachable-subgraph inequations (as in CompCert's `fixpoint_nodeset_solution`) at the cost of violating inequations on edges out of unreachable nodes when transfers are non-strict (not proved here). Entry-only seeding is not formalized here.
Without monotone transfers the solver can return a solution that is not least (kildall_needs_monotone); termination and the solution property do not need monotonicity.
It says nothing about MOP; see kildall-computes-mop for the end-to-end statement under distributivity and the exactness side conditions.

All-nodes worklist seeding vs entry-only seeding trades global inequation satisfaction against unreachable-code isolation: seeding all nodes (`kildall`) guarantees a global `IsSolution` without strictness (even without monotonicity, `kildall_isSolution_of_eq_some`) but allows non-strict unreachable nodes to over-approximate reachable nodes (`exactness_needs_unreachableStrict`), whereas seeding only the entry avoids unreachable-node propagation and solves the reachable-subgraph inequations (as in CompCert's `fixpoint_nodeset_solution`) at the cost of violating inequations on edges out of unreachable nodes when transfers are non-strict (not proved here). Entry-only seeding is not formalized here.

One unit of `fuel` in `kildall` pays for popping one node `u` and running `propagate` across all entries of `succs G u`; thus `fuel ≥ n * (h + 1) + 1` bounds outer worklist pops rather than individual edge propagations (`O(|G.edges|)` join and order checks per pop, including duplicate edges).

It does not establish semantic soundness with respect to any concrete operational semantics: `MOP ≤ x` only relates solutions of the abstract inequations to syntactic compositions of the given transfer functions `G.f`, without proving that `G.f` soundly abstracts concrete program execution.

`MOP` ranges over all syntactically valid CFG walks `Walk G v`, including dynamically infeasible branch combinations; `MFP = MOP` therefore does not mean exactness with respect to feasible runtime executions (a join over only the feasible paths).

`x v` and `IsMOPAt L G v` represent pre-transfer facts at node entry (`MFP◦` and `MOP◦`), because `G.f u` is applied only along outgoing edges `(u, w) ∈ G.edges`; at any sink or return node `v` with zero outgoing edges, `G.f v` is completely unconstrained and ignored unless a synthetic exit edge `(v, exit)` is added.

`CFG` applies a single node-indexed transfer `G.f u` along every outgoing edge of `u` and assumes a single entry node `G.entry` (`n ≥ 1`); branch-sensitive edge transfers `(u, w) ↦ f_{u,w}` and multi-entry graphs require edge-splitting or a synthetic super-entry node.
prior_art: G. A. Kildall, "A unified approach to global program optimization", Conference Record of the ACM Symposium on Principles of Programming Languages (POPL 1973), pp. 194-206, doi:10.1145/512927.512945 (public-domain archival copy: handle 10945/42162). Works over a finite meet-semilattice with transfer functions having the 'homomorphism property' f(N, x ^ y) = f(N, x) ^ f(N, y) (distributivity, in the dual orientation); Algorithm A is a worklist algorithm; Theorem 1 states that it terminates; Theorem 2 relates the final pool at each node N to the values propagated along all paths from entry nodes to N. Exact bounds and formulas of the paper are not quoted here.

J. B. Kam and J. D. Ullman, "Monotone data flow analysis frameworks", Acta Informatica 7(3):305-317, 1977, doi:10.1007/BF00290339. The abstract states that the maximal fixed point solution exists for every instance of every monotone framework and is obtained by Kildall's algorithm; that whenever a framework is monotone but not distributive there are instances in which the meet-over-all-paths solution differs from the maximal fixed point; and that no algorithm computes the meet-over-all-paths solution for monotone frameworks in general. These statements concern monotone frameworks in general (meet-semilattice orientation); this card cites only the abstract, and attributes to the paper no statement about any particular framework such as constant propagation.

F. Nielson, H. R. Nielson, C. Hankin, Principles of Program Analysis, Springer, 1999 (corrected 2nd printing 2005), doi:10.1007/978-3-662-03811-6, ISBN 978-3-540-65410-0. Chapter 2: Section 2.3 'Monotone Frameworks' (2.3.3 'A Non-distributive Example'), Section 2.4 'Equation Solving' (2.4.1 'The MFP Solution', 2.4.2 'The MOP Solution'); worklist algorithms in Section 6.1. The authors' Chapter 2 transparencies (May 2005), slide 79, state a lemma for the MFP and MOP solutions of an instance of a monotone framework: 'MFP◦ ⊒ MOP◦ and MFP• ⊒ MOP•', and 'If the framework is distributive and if path◦(ℓ) ≠ ∅ for all ℓ in E and F then: MFP◦ = MOP◦ and MFP• = MOP•' (join orientation; MFP◦/MFP• and MOP◦/MOP• are the pre- and post-transfer solutions).

tier_justification: Prior statements exclude the situation by assuming that every node has a path from the entry (Nielson-Nielson-Hankin) or that all transfers are strict (CompCert's fixpoint_solution); the explicit three-node acyclic counterexample, in which the affected node is itself reachable, is what is made precise and checked here.
plain_claim: With gen/kill (distributive) transfers on 1-bit vectors, there is a three-node CFG (entry 0 → 2, and an unreachable node 1 with no incoming edge, gen = {0}, and an edge 1 → 2) in which node 2 is reachable from the entry, yet the least solution at node 2 is {0} while MOP there is ∅ (ugCFG_isMOPAt_two_empty).
depth_justification: Finite computation of the least solution and of the path values.
nonvacuity_witness: The instance itself (all listed properties are proved).
non_claims: It does not show that unreachable nodes always break exactness: when every unreachable node has a strict transfer, the least solution equals MOP (isMOPAt_of_isLeastSolution_of_distributive_of_unreachableStrict); in this instance the MOP value at node 2 is ∅ (ugCFG_isMOPAt_two_empty). That a non-strict unreachable node without edges into the rest of the graph is also harmless is plausible but not proved here.

Not established here: a local form of the unreachable-node condition. The package does not prove that strictness is needed only at unreachable nodes from which `v` can be reached; `UnreachableStrict` constrains every unreachable node.
It does not involve a cycle; an unreachable cycle is not needed for the failure.
It does not concern the computed fixpoint of a solver seeded only from the entry, which would not propagate from node 1 (not proved here; entry-only seeding is not formalized).

tier_justification: An instance of the classical fact that the join of the iterates f^k(⊥) is the least fixed point for continuous maps but not, in general, for maps that are merely monotone (Davey-Priestley, Chapter 8; transfinite iteration in Cousot-Cousot 1979): on the loop, MOP is the join of the iterates and MFP is the least fixed point.
plain_claim: On the chain 0 < 1 < 2 < ⋯ < ω < ω+1, which violates the ascending chain condition and on which every monotone map is distributive (omegaLat_monotone_distributive), the CFG 0 → 1 with a loop 1 → 1 whose transfer is the successor map (k ↦ k+1, ω ↦ ω+1) has all nodes reachable, distributive transfers, and least solution ω+1 at node 1, while MOP there (the least upper bound of the path values 0, 1, 2, …) is ω.
depth_justification: Path values are exactly the finite elements; the least solution is forced by the loop inequation.
non_claims: It does not show that infinite-height lattices always break exactness; ACC suffices, and lattices with ACC can have unbounded height (acc_strictly_weaker_than_heightLe, exactness_holds_on_unboundedChainsLat). A transfer that is continuous at the limit (here, mapping ω to ω) would not produce this gap (not proved here).
A variant with all transfers strict is strict_exactness_needs_acc.

It does not concern termination of a solver (non-termination on this lattice is not proved here; kildall_needs_heightLe proves that the solver returns none for every fuel on the successor self-loop succCFG over natMaxLat).

`AscendingChainCondition` (sufficient for `mfp-eq-mop-exactness`) is strictly weaker than uniform finite height `HeightLe h` (assumed by the uniform fuel bound in `kildall_isSome_of_heightLe`; under the ascending chain condition alone no uniform fuel bound exists, `kildall_acc_has_no_uniform_fuel`); neither theorem models widening (`∇`) or narrowing (`Δ`) operators used on infinite-height domains. Lean: `acc_strictly_weaker_than_heightLe`, `exactness_holds_on_unboundedChainsLat`, `kildall_acc_has_no_uniform_fuel`.
